t: Musa ruled the Mali Empire at its territorial peak, when its wealth came from taxing and controlling the trade in salt and in gold from Bambuk and Bure.

His pilgrimage of 1324–1325, with an enormous entourage and a vast supply of gold, made him known across North Africa and the Middle East, and most of what is known of him comes from Arabic writers who recorded it.
Arabic authors praised his generosity and justice, while Mandé oral tradition gives him little space and some of its performers say he wasted Mali's wealth.
dyk: Musa encouraged the belief that his wealth was inexhaustible by spreading rumours that gold grew like a plant in his kingdom. On the way home from Mecca he nonetheless ran out of money and had to borrow from Egyptian merchants.
ev: Musa becomes Mansa of Mali under unclear circumstances; by his own account his predecessor never returned from an expedition into the Atlantic Ocean
On his way to Mecca he reaches the outskirts of Cairo in July, meets the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad and stays three months, giving and spending freely
He completes the hajj; on the return to Cairo many of his pilgrims die of cold, starvation or bandit raids, and he goes into debt to merchants
The kingdom of Mossi invades and conquers Timbuktu; Musa regains the city, builds a rampart and stone fort and stations a standing army there
According to Ibn Khaldun, he sends an envoy to congratulate Abu al-Hasan Ali on the conquest of Tlemcen, which took place in May of that year
Musa dies; the date is uncertain, and by other reckonings he died in 1332 or earlier

f.born: c. 1280; the date is unknown, but he appears to have been a young man in 1324; of the Keita dynasty of Mali, a descendant of Abu Bakr, brother of Sunjata, though his parentage is disputed
f.died: c. 1337; the date is uncertain: 1332 or earlier by some reckonings, 1337 regarded as most likely by Nehemia Levtzion; place and manner are not recorded
f.role: Ninth Mansa (ruler) of the Mali Empire, from the early 1300s until his death
f.known: his hajj to Mecca in 1324–1325; lavish gifts of gold in Cairo; bringing Gao and Timbuktu into the Mali Empire; recruiting scholars such as Abu Ishaq al-Sahili; building in Timbuktu, including part of Djinguereber Mosque; a lasting reputation for fabulous wealth
